newsitem.title: USA: Inflation-index bond sale set for Jan--US Treasury.
newsitem.headline: Inflation-index bond sale set for Jan--US Treasury.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury Department official said the department will hold its first auction for inflation-indexed securities in January and plans to issue 10-year notes.

"The first auction is in January. We will start with the 10-year note," said U.S. Treasury Deputy Assistant Secretary for Federal Finance Roger Anderson, while speaking in New York at a Lehman Brothers luncheon.
He added that the Treasury will re-open that 10-year note until the issue is of sufficient size.
He said the Department plans to auction a second issue sometime next year.
"We will be able to issue the second maturity in 1997," Anderson said. He said at this time, the Treasury was not sure whether the maturity of securities in that issue would be longer than 10 years.
"We expect to issue in the first couple of years several maturities shorter and longer than 10 years," he added.
Anderson said the U.S. securities will mirror the Canadian model of inflation-indexed instruments.

"The structure is that we will be following the Canadian model whereby on a daily basis, the principal of these securities will be adjusted for inflation," Anderson said, adding the inflation adjustment will be paid at maturity.
Anderson said the securities will be "strippable" in January.
He also addressed concerns many investors have expressed in the past over whether the inflation-indexed security market will be large enough for liquidity purposes.
"We are committed to a substantial market," Anderson said.
These instruments will be linked to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as calculated by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Anderson said the securities will incorporate any technical or professional changes the BLS might make in calculating the CPI.
However, if Congress were to mandate a change in how the index were calculated, Anderson said the Treasury would then pick a different price index.

"If Congress were to actually change how CPI is calculated, we will come up with a substitute index. What we are saying is that we're going to protect people from the political risk of Congress changing CPI," he said.
